title: The Grand Budapest Hotel
synopsis: A concierge, a lobby boy, an inheritance scandal, a painting of a boy with an apple, and a long sled ride down an alpine slope.

nodes.text: A boy of indeterminate age stands at your desk with a folded cap and an application filled out in three different pens. Experience: none. Education: none. Family: none. He has written the word zero in every blank, and it is also, he explains, his name. You look at him for a full three seconds.

choices.consequence: You hire him on the spot at a wage of nothing plus a bunk, and he thanks you as though you handed him a country. You choose to hire him. By Madame D., the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You inform him the position requires consideration, then have him polishing brass within the hour, because nobody else turned up. You choose to defer. By Madame D., the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Madame Céline D., eighty-four, arrives in the lobby in full fur and full panic, gripping your sleeve. She has had a premonition. She will not be back. She presses a small brass key into your palm and tells you which of her sons she is most afraid of, and it turns out to be all of them.

choices.consequence: You walk her out to the car, adjust her collar, and assure her nothing has ever once happened to a guest of this hotel. You reassure her. It gets you to Will Reading, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You keep your voice level and your hands behind your back, and she watches you the entire way to the door, waiting. You choose to be cold. By Will Reading, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The drawing room contains nine relatives, four lawyers, and a notary reading at the speed of frost. Then comes the codicil. Your name, in a will, between a shipping concern and a set of Bohemian glass. The room turns as one body. Somebody's dog begins, very quietly, to growl.

choices.consequence: You say you are honored and you mean it, and every heir present immediately reclassifies you as a legal problem to be solved. You accept it. It gets you to Boy With Apple, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You decline aloud, which convinces nobody, since the painting is worth more than the province and every person in the room knows it. You refuse. It gets you to Boy With Apple, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: It is not large: a boy, an apple, a background the color of weak tea, and a valuation that would buy this hotel twice over. It hangs in the second drawing room beneath a lamp. Everyone in the house would kill for it, and one of them is currently offering you brandy.

choices.consequence: You lift it off the wall, hang a lurid nude in its place, and walk out through a funeral with it under your coat. You choose to steal it. By Dmitri, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You leave it where it is for six more hours, which is five hours and fifty minutes longer than is survivable. You commit to wait. The road to Dmitri is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The son wears black leather indoors and travels with a servant called Jopling, whose knuckles are decorated and whose coat is cut to hold objects. Dmitri accuses you of things in the corridor, loudly and mostly accurately. Jopling says nothing. Jopling is holding a cat, for no reason anyone can determine.

choices.consequence: You call him something unrepeatable in three languages and land one clean punch before Jopling separates you like laundry. You choose to antagonize him. By Train, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You apologize with tremendous grace for nothing you did. Dmitri accepts the apology. The cat is dead by morning. You choose to placate him. By Train, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The compartment door opens and there are six of them and they want papers. Zero's permit was issued by a country that no longer exists. Hands go to his collar. Then an officer in the corridor looks at your face and lowers his lamp, because thirty years ago you carried his mother's luggage up four flights.

choices.consequence: You put yourself between a boy and six rifles armed with nothing but impeccable diction, and it works, which astonishes everyone including you.

You hold your tongue and count the seconds, and Zero's collar is already torn by the time the officer recognizes your face. You commit to stay still. The road to Police Order is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Poison from the strychnine family, a solicitor missing two fingers, and a telegram with your name spelled correctly, which is somehow the worst part of it. Two constables are at the desk asking for discretion. Behind them, guests are pretending to read newspapers upside down. You have ninety seconds and one exit.

choices.consequence: You go with them holding your own elbow, requesting only that they not use the front stairs in view of the guests. You surrender quietly. It gets you to Prison Cell, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You get through the kitchens, across the courtyard, and some way up a drainpipe before a gardener takes both your ankles. You choose to bolt. By Prison Cell, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Checkpoint Nineteen. Your cellmate wears a world map inked across his back, out of date by two borders, and he has been here long enough to hold firm opinions about the gruel. He is planning something. He shows you a sketch drawn on the back of a soap wrapper, and the sketch is very good.

choices.consequence: You divide one courtesan au chocolat five ways among the most violent men in Lutz and purchase an escape with it. You choose to trade pastries for tools. By Mendl's Box, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You hold off and leave the pastry intact on the shelf, and four hardened criminals guard it for three days like a shrine. You commit to wait. The road to Mendl's Box is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The parcel is tied with the ribbon, and nobody searches a Mendl's box; the guards would sooner search a cathedral. Inside the mille-feuille, arranged so carefully that the layers still stand, are a hammer, a chisel, and a file. The pastry is undamaged. She is nineteen and she is extraordinary.

choices.consequence: You start on the floor stones that night, and Ludwig weeps openly, and later denies it in front of the others. You use it. It gets you to Sewer Run, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You slide the tools under the mattress to wait for the right night, and eat the pastry, because not eating it would be a crime. You save it. It gets you to Sewer Run, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Down the shaft, through a grate, and into a river of everything Lutz has ever been ashamed of. The pipe narrows at the third junction. Ludwig goes first. You go third, holding a handkerchief over your face with one hand and your dignity with the other. Overhead, boots cross the square in sixes.

choices.consequence: You take it at a sprint and reach the outfall filthy, gasping, and a good forty minutes ahead of the alarm. You commit to run. The road to Society of the Crossed Keys is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You go slowly and quietly and arrive intact, having composed, entirely in your head, a formal complaint about municipal drainage. You crawl. It gets you to Society of the Crossed Keys, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You telephone the number nobody writes down. A concierge in Ober answers mid-check-in, listens for two seconds, and puts you on hold. Then a concierge in Nebelsbad, then one in a fishing town nobody has heard of. Across four countries, men in identical purple abandon their desks and reach for their receivers.

choices.consequence: You ask for a car, a disguise, and a monastery, and receive all three plus a packed lunch inside the hour. You commit to call them. The road to Monastery is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You hesitate over the receiver for a full minute out of pride, then dial anyway, because pride has never once run a switchboard. You commit to wait. The road to Monastery is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You have him by both hands in a cold stone chamber. Serge X. has been hiding in a mountain monastery in a borrowed habit, singing bass badly. He knows what was in the second will and whose hand held the pen. He will tell you everything. He gets four sentences out before the choir starts and drowns him completely.

choices.consequence: You hold his hands and tell him he is safe here, which is a lie the two of you accept for ninety seconds. You reassure him. It gets you to Sled Chase, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You raise your voice inside a house of God and regret it instantly, and he tells you anyway, out of fright. You threaten him. It gets you to Sled Chase, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: A wooden toboggan, a mountain, and Jopling on skis behind you doing something with a knife that suggests practice. Zero steers. You do not steer; you hold on and shout corrections nobody can hear. The track forks at a cliff edge, one branch has a signpost, and neither of you can read it in time.

choices.consequence: You take the inside line through pine trees and lose your hat, both gloves, and a structural portion of the toboggan. You choose to cut a corner. By Boy With Apple, Again, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You stay on the groomed track and let him gain, betting everything on the bottom bend being tighter than he expects. You commit to hold the line. The road to Boy With Apple, Again is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: It has been in your suite the whole time, behind a canvas of two nudes and a hoop that you selected precisely because nobody would look at it twice. You lift it out. The apple is still there. So is the boy, and his expression has not improved with the political situation.

choices.consequence: You carry it downstairs under your arm, in daylight, past soldiers, on the theory that confidence is a form of paperwork. You choose to reveal it. By Lobby Coup, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You get as far as naming a figure to a dealer in Lutz, then wrap it back up and take it home. You sell it. It gets you to Lobby Coup, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: The lobby has a checkpoint in it. A trestle table stands where the flower arrangement was, a corporal has a stamp, and the piano has been shifted to make room for a filing cabinet. The bellhops are still working. That is the part that stops you halfway down the stairs.

choices.consequence: You cross the lobby complaining loudly about the flowers, the corporal apologizes to you, and you do not break stride. You choose to bluff. By Train, Again, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You take the service stair with the painting flat against your chest, listening to your own hotel being reorganized below you. You hide. It gets you to Train, Again, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Different train, same compartment, and this time nobody in the corridor was ever a small boy in your lobby. The officer checking Zero's papers has a scar, a promotion, and a great deal less patience than the last one. There is a password. You have about a second to decide whether it still means anything.

choices.consequence: You say the phrase clearly, to a stranger, in a corridor, staking a boy's life on a fraternity of doormen. You choose to speak the password. By Will Hidden, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You say nothing and let the papers speak, and the papers are worth precisely as much as the country that issued them. You choose to stay quiet. By Will Hidden, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: There is an envelope taped inside the frame, behind the boy's head, where it has sat since before you knew her sons' names. Second testament. In the event of my murder. Her handwriting slopes uphill at the end of every line, exactly as it did on hotel cards for thirty years.

choices.consequence: You read it standing up, in a full room, in front of witnesses, in the voice you use for announcing dinner. You commit to read it aloud. The road to Pastry Shop is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You hold one corner to the lamp for two seconds and take it back, because she wrote it for exactly this morning. You commit to burn it. The road to Pastry Shop is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Flour to the elbows, a birthmark shaped like Mexico, and a piping bag she puts down for nobody. She has carried stolen evidence in a cake box across a militarized border. Zero produces a ring he cannot afford, in front of you, at the counter, and she keeps piping with the other hand while she says yes.

choices.consequence: You give them thirty seconds and stand there holding your hat like a man at somebody else's wedding, which you are. You choose to hold the moment. By Roof, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You clap once, congratulate them both in a single sentence, and are through the door before the door has finished closing. You commit to run. The road to Roof is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: A snowbound observatory, a stone parapet, and Jopling coming across the ice toward you with those knuckles. Zero hits him from behind with something and it barely registers. You finish with both hands in his coat at the very edge, and the drop is long, and he is not a large man to shift.

choices.consequence: You push, and a man goes off a mountain, and you discover you are able to straighten your jacket afterwards. You push. It gets you to Council Room, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You try to haul him back over the parapet out of an instinct you could not defend in court, and the ice decides it. You hold him. It gets you to Council Room, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: The second testament is read out in a room with a stenographer, and it takes seven minutes to hand you a hotel, a fortune, and the boy with the apple. Dmitri stands up twice. The lawyers hold him down by the sleeves. At the back of the room Zero is crying and claiming to have a cold.

choices.consequence: You send for something absurd in three bottles and toast a dead woman by name, in front of her sons, at length. You toast. It gets you to Last Train, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You keep your hands folded and your face shut, and only Zero notices that you have not blinked in some time. You commit to stay solemn. The road to Last Train is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The train halts in a wheat field with no station. Boots in the corridor again, and this time the officer is young, has no idea who you are, and there is no lamp lowered and no password worth saying. Zero's papers are in your hand. You are sitting between him and the door.

choices.consequence: You stand, put yourself in the aisle, and address a boy holding a rifle exactly as you would address a guest. You commit to stand. The road to Pink Hotel, Glorious Dawn is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You stay seated and keep your voice low and reasonable, and reasonable has a much shorter reach than it used to. You commit to sit down. The road to Zero Tells the Story is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

There is one other way out of this compartment, and it has been in your breast pocket since the monastery. You commit to take the third path. The road to Boy With Apple on the Wall is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You run the Grand Budapest for four more seasons and it is, briefly, glorious again: the lift works, the orchestra comes back, the trout is beyond reproach. Zero takes the desk after you and never once changes the flowers you chose. Agatha bakes something every year on the anniversary of the will reading, and grown men eat it on the lobby steps and have to study the ceiling.

Decades on, in a hotel with orange carpet and a lift that sticks, an old man buys a young writer dinner and talks for three hours. He describes cologne, a pencil mustache, a poem recited during a gunfight, and a manner of speaking that belonged to a world already finished. He keeps one suite he never sleeps in. The writer asks why. He says he keeps it for her.

The painting stays where you hung it, over the mantel in your own rooms, lit properly, dusted weekly by a boy who will one day own the building. Dmitri ends his years in two rooms in Lutz with a postcard reproduction propped against the clock, telling anyone who sits still long enough that it was stolen from him by a hotel employee. This is, technically, correct.
